novel_actions_proposed.label: defer_new_purchase_explore_alternatives
novel_actions_proposed.description: Rather than buying a new computer by cutting essentials, the parent proposes first exhausting lower-risk alternatives (used devices, school loaner programs, library access) before committing to a purchase that threatens household stability.

novel_actions_proposed.label: leverage_school_community_resources
novel_actions_proposed.description: The teacher/tutor recommends connecting the family with school-based or community resources (loaner devices, digital equity programs, after-school lab access) as a bridge solution that avoids cutting essentials.

novel_actions_proposed.label: staged_harm_minimizing_acquisition
novel_actions_proposed.description: The advisor recommends a structured, harm-minimizing approach: first assess whether essentials remain fully covered, then pursue subsidized or low-cost device options, and only proceed with a new purchase if it does not materially endanger food, housing, utilities, or healthcare.

synthesis_description: All three agents converge on the position that essential expenses (housing, food, utilities, healthcare, transportation) must not be compromised for a new computer purchase; instead, the family should actively pursue alternative access routes—such as school loaner programs, community digital equity initiatives, used devices, or library resources—before considering any purchase, and only proceed with buying if basic stability is demonstrably preserved.
points_of_disagreement: The degree of urgency assigned to digital access as an educational necessity versus a supplementary convenience varies slightly between agents.
The parent-protagonist emphasizes the compounding financial risk of cutting essentials most strongly, while the teacher focuses more on the visible classroom spillover of household instability.
The external advisor is most explicit about requiring a formal budget assessment before any purchase decision, while the other agents treat this more implicitly.
summary: All three agents—the parent, the community teacher, and the external advisor—reject a straightforward 'buy the new computer by cutting essentials' framing (ACTION_1) without also rejecting the idea that educational access matters. None advocates for simple inaction (ACTION_2) either. Instead, they converge on a synthesis position: essential expenses are non-negotiable as a baseline, and the family should first exhaust alternative routes to digital access (school loaners, community programs, used devices, library labs) before considering any new purchase. If and only if a purchase can be made without materially endangering housing, food, utilities, healthcare, or transportation should it proceed. The shared ethical logic across all agents is that destabilizing the household undermines the very educational continuity the computer is meant to support, making harm-minimization and resource-seeking the most defensible path forward.
